trails.trailTip: The maintained trail ends at the toe of the glacier — hidden crevasses and slick ice make traveling further onto Root Glacier without microspikes and, ideally, a local guide genuinely dangerous, not just uncomfortable.
trails.didYouKnow: Root Glacier is a tributary of the much larger Kennicott Glacier, and both are actively retreating, visibly reshaping the valley year to year.

trails.trailTip: There's no water treatment or facilities along the route — carry all the water you'll need or a filter, and start early since the exposed upper switchbacks offer no shelter from afternoon weather.
trails.didYouKnow: The Bonanza Mine ruins sit at roughly 5,865 feet, marking one of the richest copper deposits ever discovered, which financed the Kennecott mill complex below.

trails.trailTip: The route becomes faint above treeline — carry a topo map or GPS track rather than relying on cairns or tread, and expect route-finding across talus near the lake.
trails.didYouKnow: Erie Lake sits in a glacially carved cirque high above the Kennecott valley, fed by snowmelt that keeps it ice-covered well into summer.

trails.trailTip: As of September 2026, per NPS/Recreation.gov, the Nugget Creek public-use cabin requires an advance reservation to occupy overnight, though the trail itself is open for day use without any permit.
trails.didYouKnow: The cabin is a converted historic structure and one of only a handful of maintained backcountry shelters in a park with almost no other overnight infrastructure.

trails.trailTip: Many of Kennecott's mill buildings are structurally fragile — admire the historic townsite from marked paths and stay out of any structure not explicitly open for a ranger-led tour.
trails.didYouKnow: Kennecott's copper mill operated from 1911 to 1938 and was abandoned almost overnight when the ore ran out, leaving buildings largely as workers left them.

trails.trailTip: This is unmaintained above the lower mile, in prime grizzly habitat — make noise while moving through brush, carry bear spray, and be ready to navigate by map once the tread disappears.
trails.didYouKnow: Donoho Basin offers close-up views of the Root Glacier icefall from above, a perspective most visitors only see from the valley floor.

trails.trailTip: This is a multi-day wilderness traverse, not a maintained trail — most of the route has no defined tread, requires confident off-trail navigation across tundra and talus, and most parties fly in or out via a backcountry air taxi rather than walking a loop.
trails.didYouKnow: The Goat Trail follows a route originally used by prospectors and, before them, Ahtna people traveling between the coast and interior.

trails.trailTip: The climb is short but steep and rocky underfoot — trekking poles help on the loose sections near the top.
trails.didYouKnow: The overlook takes in both the Kennicott and Root Glaciers at once, along with the peaks of the Wrangell Mountains beyond.

animals.whereToLook: Steep mountain slopes visible from the McCarthy Road and higher trails
animals.viewingTip: Glass distant slopes with binoculars or a spotting scope from the road or trail rather than climbing toward a band of sheep — during the fall rut, rams are focused on each other and easily disturbed by close approach.
animals.didYouKnow: Dall sheep are the only wild white sheep in North America and rely on the sharp contrast against dark rock to spot predators from a distance.

animals.whereToLook: River valleys and open tundra throughout the park's backcountry
animals.viewingTip: Carry bear spray, make noise while hiking in brush or near rushing water, and view any bear from at least 100 yards with binoculars — never approach a den or a sow with cubs.
animals.didYouKnow: Wrangell-St. Elias is the largest national park in the U.S. — larger than Switzerland — giving its grizzlies some of the most contiguous wild habitat left in North America.

animals.whereToLook: Open tundra and valley migration routes
animals.viewingTip: View migrating herds from a distance with binoculars or a scope, and give extra space during the May-June calving season when cows with newborn calves are especially easily stressed by human presence.
animals.didYouKnow: Caribou in this region can migrate well over a hundred miles between seasonal ranges, one of the longest land migrations in North America.

animals.viewingTip: Watch from below with binoculars or a scope rather than climbing toward a goat on a cliff face — startled goats can dislodge rock onto themselves or hikers below.
animals.didYouKnow: Mountain goats have specialized rubbery hoof pads that grip bare rock, letting them stand on slopes far steeper than they look able to climb.

animals.whereToLook: Cottonwoods along the park's glacial rivers
animals.viewingTip: Watch nesting pairs from the riverbank with binoculars rather than approaching the nest tree — give the area a wide berth during the April-July nesting window.
animals.didYouKnow: Bald eagles here often nest in the tallest cottonwoods along braided glacial rivers, giving them a clear line of sight for hunting salmon and waterfowl.

animals.viewingTip: Lynx are almost never seen directly — look for tracks or sign in snow rather than seeking out a den, and never approach or linger near one if you find it.
animals.didYouKnow: Lynx populations rise and fall in multi-year cycles tied closely to snowshoe hare abundance, their primary prey.

animals.viewingTip: Watch lodges and dams from shore at dusk with binoculars — approaching or disturbing a lodge can cause beavers to abandon an otherwise good site.
animals.didYouKnow: Beaver dams throughout the park's lowlands create wetland habitat that in turn supports moose, waterfowl, and fish.

animals.whereToLook: Alpine meadows and tundra along high trails
animals.viewingTip: Enjoy watching them from a normal trail distance, but never feed them — human food disrupts the fat reserves they need to survive up to eight months of hibernation.
animals.didYouKnow: Arctic ground squirrels can lower their body temperature below freezing during hibernation, the most extreme cold tolerance known in any mammal.
